summary_html: Court issues a **protective or restraining order** to prevent contact, remove abuser, or ensure safety without removing the child. Federal law leaves implementation to states but funds protection efforts through CAPTA and IV-B.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — authorizes protective interventions and state plan requirements  
- **SSA Title IV-B** — permits funding for protective services and court interventions

primary_citations.citation_text: New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 411 et seq. (Child Protective Services Act – reporting requirements)
New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Second Department
key_cases.holding: Reaching the merits under the mootness exception and reversing, the Second Department held that a parent excluded from the home by a full stay-away order of protection in an article 10 proceeding is entitled to a prompt Family Court Act § 1028 hearing applying the imminent-risk standard, because such an order is functionally equivalent to removal of the children from his care.
key_cases.relevance: This is the leading published New York authority on the due process consequences of an exclusionary order of protection.
key_cases.quote: it must be governed by the same legal standards as are provided for removal of a child in Family Court Act §§ 1027 and 1028

key_cases.holding: Answering certified questions from the Second Circuit, the Court of Appeals held that a child's exposure to domestic violence does not alone establish neglect or justify removal, that neglect requires a preponderance showing of actual or imminent impairment caused by the parent's failure to exercise a minimum degree of care, and that emergency removal without a court order under Family Court Act § 1024 is permissible only where the danger is so urgent that there is no time to obtain an ex parte order.
key_cases.relevance: Nicholson identifies court-ordered exclusion of the offending adult as an alternative to removing the child from the home.
key_cases.quote: emergency removal is appropriate where the danger is so immediate, so urgent that the child's life or safety will be at risk before an ex parte order can be obtained

key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, First Department
key_cases.holding: The First Department held that Family Court may grant a suspended judgment retroactively after a parent has completed the terms of a dispositional order, vacating the neglect finding and dismissing the petition where that serves the children's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: The children returned home only after the abusive partner was excluded, illustrating exclusion as the safety measure that permits reunification.
key_cases.quote: Family Court Act § 1051 (c) authorizes dismissal upon two separate and distinct grounds

timeline_requirements.deadline: No later than the next court day after the petition is filed
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Petition filed after a removal without a court order
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in statute (the hearing continues on successive court days until the court decides)

What is the specific imminent danger?
Where are you taking my child?
what_not_to_do: Do not physically interfere with lawful removal
